:::{#thm-fubini-tonelli}

#### Fubini--Tonelli theorem (measure-theoretic form)

Let $(\Omega_1, \mathcal F_1, \mu_1)$ and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal F_2, \mu_2)$
be **$\sigma$-finite** measure spaces,
and let $f : \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be measurable
with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebra
$\mathcal F_1 \otimes \mathcal F_2$.
If either

(a) $f \ge 0$ almost everywhere with respect to $\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2$
(**Tonelli's theorem**), or

(b) $\int_{\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2} \abs{f}\,d(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2) < \infty$
(**Fubini's theorem**),

then both iterated integrals exist, agree with the double integral,
and equal each other:

$$
\ba
\int_{\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2} f\,d(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)
&= \int_{\Omega_1} \paren{\int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2)\,d\mu_2(\omega_2)}\,d\mu_1(\omega_1)\\
&= \int_{\Omega_2} \paren{\int_{\Omega_1} f(\omega_1, \omega_2)\,d\mu_1(\omega_1)}\,d\mu_2(\omega_2).
\ea
$$

[@billingsley1995probability, Theorem 18.3; @gut2013, Theorem 9.1, p. 65;
@fubini1907; @wp:fubini]

:::


{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-fubini-tonelli-probability}
#### Fubini--Tonelli for probability measures

Applied courses rarely need the measure-theoretic generalization itself,
but it is what justifies the
[joint-distribution form](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#cor-fubini-joint)
corollary in
*Probability for Data Science*.
A probability measure gives the whole space measure $1$,
so it is finite, and hence $\sigma$-finite;
for probability measures, the $\sigma$-finiteness condition is automatic.

The integrability conditions
(nonnegativity or absolute integrability) still need to be verified
in each application.
For example, Lebesgue measure (ordinary length) on $[0, 1]$ is a probability measure,
so the $\sigma$-finiteness condition holds for both factors $[0, 1]$,
yet the two iterated integrals in @exm-fubini-fail
are $\pi/4$ and $-\pi/4$.
So $\sigma$-finiteness alone does not make the iterated integrals agree.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-fubini-tonelli-apply}

#### Positive application of @thm-fubini-tonelli

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent $\operatorname{Exponential}(1)$
[random variables](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-random-variable),
with [joint density](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pdf)
$f(x, y) = e^{-(x+y)}$ for $x, y \ge 0$.


The probability $P(X \le 1,\, Y \le 1)$
is the integral of $f$ over $[0, 1]^2$
with respect to Lebesgue measure (ordinary length) in each coordinate.
Lebesgue measure on $[0, \infty)$ is $\sigma$-finite,
because $[0, \infty)$ is the union of the intervals $[0, n]$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
each of finite length $n$;
so the $\sigma$-finiteness condition of @thm-fubini-tonelli holds.
Since $f(x,y) = e^{-(x+y)} \ge 0$,
condition (a) (Tonelli's theorem, nonnegativity) is also satisfied.

By @thm-fubini-tonelli, both iterated integrals exist and agree.
Integrating $y$ first, then $x$:

$$
\ba
P(X \le 1,\, Y \le 1)
&= \int_0^1\!\int_0^1 e^{-(x+y)}\,dy\,dx
\\&= \int_0^1\!\int_0^1 e^{-x} e^{-y}\,dy\,dx
&& \text{(exponential of a sum)}
\\&= \int_0^1 e^{-x}\paren{\int_0^1 e^{-y}\,dy}\,dx
&& \text{(} e^{-x} \text{ is constant in } y \text{)}
\\&= \int_0^1 e^{-x}\sb{-e^{-y}}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx
&& \text{(antiderivative of } e^{-y} \text{)}
\\&= \int_0^1 e^{-x}(1 - e^{-1})\,dx
&& \text{(evaluate at the limits)}
\\&= (1 - e^{-1})\int_0^1 e^{-x}\,dx
&& \text{(} 1 - e^{-1} \text{ is constant in } x \text{)}
\\&= (1 - e^{-1})\sb{-e^{-x}}_{x=0}^{x=1}
&& \text{(antiderivative of } e^{-x} \text{)}
\\&= (1 - e^{-1})^2
&& \text{(evaluate at the limits)}
\ea
$$

Integrating $x$ first, then $y$:

$$
\ba
P(X \le 1,\, Y \le 1)
&= \int_0^1\!\int_0^1 e^{-(x+y)}\,dx\,dy
\\&= \int_0^1\!\int_0^1 e^{-y} e^{-x}\,dx\,dy
&& \text{(exponential of a sum)}
\\&= \int_0^1 e^{-y}\paren{\int_0^1 e^{-x}\,dx}\,dy
&& \text{(} e^{-y} \text{ is constant in } x \text{)}
\\&= \int_0^1 e^{-y}\sb{-e^{-x}}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,dy
&& \text{(antiderivative of } e^{-x} \text{)}
\\&= \int_0^1 e^{-y}(1 - e^{-1})\,dy
&& \text{(evaluate at the limits)}
\\&= (1 - e^{-1})\int_0^1 e^{-y}\,dy
&& \text{(} 1 - e^{-1} \text{ is constant in } y \text{)}
\\&= (1 - e^{-1})\sb{-e^{-y}}_{y=0}^{y=1}
&& \text{(antiderivative of } e^{-y} \text{)}
\\&= (1 - e^{-1})^2
&& \text{(evaluate at the limits)}
\ea
$$

Both iterated integrals equal $(1 - e^{-1})^2 \approx 0.400$,
as @thm-fubini-tonelli guarantees when condition (a) holds.

:::
